title: Can you copy four angles that face different ways?
description: A question from the book asks for four angles drawn facing different ways, each copied without any measurement. The same arc and the same chord copy every angle, and side side side shows each copy is equal.
teaching_notes: One idea: the copying steps do not care which way the angle faces, because an arc and a chord are only lengths. Watch for students who turn the paper and lose track of which arm is which.

source: Figure it Out (copying an angle), Q1
video_script.why: The child has copied one angle and now checks that the method works for angles facing every direction.
video_script.substitution: The angles are copied in the same way as the example in the book: one arc, the same arc on a new ray, and the chord carried across.
video_script.anchor: Construct at least four different angles facing different ways, without taking any measurement, and make a copy of each.
video_script.payoff_line: Every copy is equal to its angle

final_answer.value: For each angle, equal arcs from A and X and the chord BC moved to ZY give ΔABC ≅ ΔXZY by SSS, so every copy is equal to its angle
final_answer.spoken: each copy uses one radius and one chord, so the triangles match by side side side and every copy is equal to its angle

never_show: the answer card before the reveal
maths_rules: Each angle is drawn with the ruler only, facing a different way: upwards, sideways, downwards and slanting.
For each angle with corner A, an arc cuts the arms at B and C; the same radius from X cuts the new ray at Z.
The chord BC is carried from Z to give Y with ZY = BC; triangle ABC is congruent to triangle XZY by SSS.
So the angle at X equals the angle at A, whichever way the angle faces.
video_script.design: One idea: the copy works in any direction. The check is the triangle pair, as in the book's example. The tracing paper check in the worklist is not in the book, so the side side side check is used.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step two, take the angle that opens upwards. Its corner is eigh.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Put the compass point on eigh, and draw an arc across both arms.

beats.on_screen: Step 3: draw a new ray from a point X; with the same radius, an arc from X cuts the ray at Z

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step three, draw a new ray from a point X anywhere on the page.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>Keep the same radius, and draw a long arc from X.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>It cuts the ray at Z.

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step four, open the compass to the length B C.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>From Z, cut the long arc at Y. Then Z Y equals B C. Join X and Y.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>Repeat all this for the other three angles.

beats.on_screen: Step 5 (check): in triangles ABC and XZY, AB = XZ, AC = XY, BC = ZY; SSS gives angle YXZ = angle CAB, for each of the four angles

marks.m2: the three pairs of equal sides light up
marks.m3: the angles at eigh and X get matching arcs in all four pictures

narration: <bookmark mark='m1'/>Step five, check the result. Triangles eigh B C and X Z Y have three pairs of equal sides.
<bookmark mark='m2'/>They are congruent by side side side, so the angle at X equals the angle at eigh.
<bookmark mark='m3'/>The same holds for all four angles, however they face.
